title: How does virtual-thread pinning happen (blocking I/O inside a `synchronized` block pins the carrier thread), and why replace `synchronized` with `ReentrantLock` in virtual-thread-heavy code?
shortTitle: How does virtual-thread pinning happen, and why replace synchronized with ReentrantLock in virtual-thread-heavy code?
keyPoints: Virtual threads unmount from carrier threads when they block on I/O, allowing the carrier to run other virtual threads.
Pinning occurs when a virtual thread blocks inside a synchronized block or method, because the monitor is tied to the carrier platform thread.
While pinned, the carrier is consumed and cannot serve other virtual threads, reducing the scalability benefit.
Replacing synchronized with ReentrantLock avoids pinning because ReentrantLock uses Java-level data structures that allow the virtual thread to unmount.
Detect pinning with the JDK Flight Recorder jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event or diagnostic output.
Never pool virtual threads because they are cheap and meant to be created one per task.
Keep critical sections small and avoid blocking I/O while holding any lock, because even ReentrantLock held across slow I/O serializes throughput.

s1_definition.oneliner: Virtual threads unmount from carriers when they block, but blocking inside synchronized pins them to the carrier and wastes it, so in virtual-thread-heavy code you replace synchronized with ReentrantLock to let the thread unmount.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Virtual thread** – A lightweight thread scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of platform carrier threads; it normally unmounts from the carrier when it blocks on I/O.
- **Pinning** – When a virtual thread cannot unmount and stays stuck to its carrier, consuming it and preventing other virtual threads from using it.
- **`synchronized` cause** – Blocking inside a `synchronized` block pins because the object monitor's ownership is recorded against the carrier platform thread.
- **`ReentrantLock` fix** – Its waiting and ownership are managed in Java-level data structures, so a virtual thread can unmount while blocked on acquisition or while holding the lock across a blocking call.
- **Detection** – Use the JDK Flight Recorder `jdk.VirtualThreadPinned` event to find pinned stacks in production.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of National Bank of India having a few senior managers (carrier threads) and thousands of tasks (virtual threads). Normally, when a task has to wait on hold for an external call, it steps aside and frees the manager to help another task. Pinning is like a task that, while holding a specific office key that only works when the original manager is present (synchronized monitor), gets stuck on a long phone call. Because the key is bound to that manager, the manager cannot leave to help anyone else and is wasted for the whole call. Switching to a ticket-based lock (ReentrantLock) lets the task keep its place in line without chaining a manager to its desk.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│         Normal Virtual Thread (unmounts)         │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                 │
│  VThread-1 mounted on Carrier-1                 │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  Hits blocking I/O (DB call)                    │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  UNMOUNTS from Carrier-1 ──→ Carrier-1 FREE     │
│  (continuation parked)       (picks up VThread-2)│
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  I/O completes ──→ Remounts on any free carrier │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│        Pinned Virtual Thread (stuck)            │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                                 │
│  VThread-1 mounted on Carrier-1                 │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  Enters synchronized block                      │
│  (monitor owned by Carrier-1)                   │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  Hits blocking I/O inside synchronized          │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  CANNOT UNMOUNT ──→ Carrier-1 STUCK             │
│  (monitor bound to carrier)  (wasted)           │
│       │                                         │
│       ▼                                         │
│  I/O completes ──→ Finally releases carrier     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Virtual threads give massive concurrency because the JVM mounts a virtual thread onto one of a small pool of platform carrier threads only while it is actually running, and when the virtual thread hits a blocking operation like socket I/O, the runtime unmounts it and lets the carrier pick up another virtual thread. The whole model depends on virtual threads yielding their carrier whenever they wait, which is how a handful of carriers can serve millions of virtual threads.

Pinning is when a virtual thread cannot unmount and stays stuck to its carrier. The classic cause is blocking inside a synchronized block or method, because the object monitor's ownership is recorded against the carrier platform thread, so the runtime cannot move the virtual thread off that carrier while it owns the monitor. When many virtual threads do this at once, they exhaust the small carrier pool and the supposedly massively concurrent service grinds to a halt.

The fix in virtual-thread-heavy code is to replace synchronized with a ReentrantLock around any critical section that contains a blocking call. A ReentrantLock keeps its waiting and ownership state in ordinary Java data structures rather than in the carrier's intrinsic monitor, so a virtual thread can unmount while it waits to acquire the lock and can unmount during a blocking call made while holding the lock, which keeps the carrier free for other work.

In banking work at National Bank of India the transfer endpoint was moved to virtual threads expecting huge concurrency, but throughput collapsed under load. A Flight Recorder capture of the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event pointed straight at a synchronized ledger method that made a blocking database call inside the monitor. Replacing the synchronized block with a ReentrantLock stopped the pinning and restored the expected scalability. The best practice is to keep critical sections tiny, do no blocking I/O while holding any lock at all, detect pinning early with Flight Recorder events, and never pool virtual threads.

Remember one sentence: blocking I/O inside synchronized pins the virtual thread to its carrier, so replace synchronized with ReentrantLock in virtual-thread-heavy code to let the thread unmount and keep the carrier free.
